Female silver gemfish (Rexea solandri) attain a maximum recorded total length of 110 centimetres [Li = 110 centimetres], a size that places them among the larger members of the family Gempylidae. Specimens approaching this ultimate length are uncommon in commercial catches, suggesting that such individuals represent older, slow-growing cohorts within the population. Body mass scales allometrically with length, and the corresponding ultimate wet weight for a female at this asymptotic size is estimated at 8919 grams [Wwi = 8919 grams]. This substantial mass supports a piscivorous diet that includes small pelagic fishes and cephalopods, consistent with an active, predatory lifestyle in the mesopelagic zone. Growth rates throughout the juvenile and sub-adult stages are influenced by both prey availability and ambient temperature, with the cool waters of the southern continental slope providing the thermal regime under which these life-history traits have evolved.

Sexual maturation in this species is marked by the attainment of a specific body size rather than a fixed chronological age. Field surveys indicate that females reach puberty at a total length of 65 centimetres [Lp = 65 centimetres], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 1710 grams [Wwp = approximately 1710 grams]. Individuals below this size are rarely found with developed gonads, implying that a minimum somatic investment is required before the onset of vitellogenesis. This length-based maturity schedule is common among temperate scombroids and likely reflects the energetic demands of the first spawning season. The transition from an immature, actively growing juvenile to a mature, reproductively viable adult involves considerable physiological reorganisation, including the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. The body mass at which this shift occurs represents a critical decision point in the species' life cycle.

Reproductive output in silver gemfish has been characterised under controlled laboratory conditions that approximate the thermal habitat of the species. At a stable water temperature of 10.4 °C [T = 10.4 °C], females produce approximately 4 million eggs per year [Ri = approximately 4 million eggs per year], released over multiple spawning events. This annual fecundity is among the highest recorded for a gempylid of this body size and reflects a reproductive strategy that relies on high egg production to offset substantial losses during the pelagic larval phase. The actual release occurs in discrete batches throughout the spawning season. The thermal regime of 10.4 °C [T = 10.4 °C] is critical for successful gametogenesis and may limit the southern distributional range of the species.

The extremely small size at birth is a notable feature of the early life history of silver gemfish. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae have an estimated wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams], a value derived from an egg diameter of one millimetre, which is typical for pelagic spawners in the family. This minuscule initial mass means the larvae are entirely dependent on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-hatching, with the lecithotrophic phase lasting until the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding begins. The transparent, chorionate embryo develops rapidly within the incubating egg, and upon hatching, the prolarva measures only a few millimetres in total length. Survival through this critical period is strongly influenced by water temperature and the timing of first prey availability.

Maximum longevity in silver gemfish has been estimated from both mark-recapture studies and otolith-based ageing analyses. Under the thermal conditions typical of their habitat, sustained at 10.4 °C [T = 10.4 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan reaches approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years]. This lifespan is considerable for a fast-growing, highly fecund mesopelagic predator and suggests that individuals can experience multiple spawning seasons over their lifetime, consistent with an iteroparous reproductive schedule. Compared to other gempylids of similar body size, the 16-year lifespan of Rexea solandri is notably extended, suggesting a slower life-history pace than in related species. The oldest documented individuals in commercial bycatch samples have been aged at nearly 5,840 days [am = nearly 5,840 days], indicating that senescence-related mortality does not become a dominant demographic force until after the first decade of life at a temperature of 10.4 °C [T = 10.4 °C]. Such longevity, combined with late maturity relative to body size, makes the species potentially vulnerable to overfishing of larger, older cohorts.
